title: Medical Bacteriology
description: Identification of medically important bacteria — staphylococci, streptococci, enterobacteria, Gram-negative non-fermenters, mycobacteria and anaerobes — and antimicrobial susceptibility testing.

topics.title: Gram-Positive Cocci
topics.summary: Staphylococci and streptococci: identification tests and diseases.

notes.b: Staphylococci are Gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase-positive. Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase-positive, often β-haemolytic with golden colonies, and ferments mannitol (yellow on mannitol salt agar). It causes boils, abscesses, wound infections, osteomyelitis (commonest cause), septic arthritis, pneumonia, endocarditis in drug users, food poisoning (preformed heat-stable enterotoxin, onset 1–6 hours), toxic shock syndrome (TSST-1) and scalded skin syndrome. Coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis — device and line infections; S. saprophyticus — urinary tract infection in young women, novobiocin-resistant).
k: S. aureus: commonest cause of osteomyelitis

notes.b: Streptococci are catalase-negative Gram-positive cocci in chains or pairs, classified by haemolysis and Lancefield groups. β-haemolytic group A (S. pyogenes — bacitracin-sensitive, PYR-positive) causes pharyngitis, impetigo, cellulitis, necrotising fasciitis, and post-streptococcal rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis. Group B (S. agalactiae — CAMP-positive, hippurate hydrolysis) causes neonatal sepsis and meningitis. α-haemolytic S. pneumoniae (lancet-shaped diplococci, optochin-sensitive, bile-soluble, capsulated) causes pneumonia, otitis media and meningitis; viridans streptococci (optochin-resistant) cause subacute endocarditis. Enterococci (group D, grow in 6.5% NaCl and bile–aesculin) cause UTI and endocarditis.
k: Group B: neonatal sepsis; CAMP test

topics.title: Enterobacteriaceae
topics.summary: Lactose fermenters and non-fermenters, biochemical identification, and diseases including typhoid.

notes.b: Enterobacteriaceae (Enterobacterales) are Gram-negative bacilli that are oxidase-negative, ferment glucose and reduce nitrate. On MacConkey agar, lactose fermenters (E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Citrobacter) are pink; non-lactose fermenters (Salmonella, Shigella, Proteus) are pale. Key tests: indole (E. coli positive), methyl red, Voges–Proskauer, citrate (IMViC: E. coli ++−−; Klebsiella −−++), urease (Proteus and Klebsiella positive), H2S on TSI or KIA (Salmonella and Proteus produce black H2S; Shigella does not), motility (Klebsiella and Shigella are non-motile; Proteus swarms). Selective media for enteric pathogens: SS agar, XLD, deoxycholate citrate agar; selenite F broth enriches Salmonella.

E. coli is the commonest cause of urinary tract infection and a cause of neonatal meningitis and diarrhoea (ETEC — travellers' diarrhoea; EHEC O157:H7 — haemolytic uraemic syndrome). Klebsiella pneumoniae causes pneumonia (in alcoholics), UTI and hospital infections; many strains produce extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBL) or carbapenemases. Salmonella Typhi causes typhoid (enteric) fever: blood culture is the best test in the first week, stool and urine cultures later; bone-marrow culture is most sensitive; the Widal test is unreliable in endemic areas. Shigella causes bacillary dysentery. Proteus mirabilis causes UTI with struvite stones (urease raises urine pH).
k: Typhoid: blood culture in week 1; Widal unreliable

topics.title: Gram-Negative Non-fermenters, Neisseria and Vibrio
topics.summary: Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Neisseria meningitidis and gonorrhoeae, and Vibrio cholerae.

notes.b: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting, strictly aerobic Gram-negative bacillus producing pigments (blue-green pyocyanin, fluorescent pyoverdin) and a grape-like odour; it grows at 42 °C. It causes infections in burns, wounds, cystic fibrosis lungs, ventilator-associated pneumonia, catheter UTIs and otitis externa, and is intrinsically resistant to many antibiotics (treated with antipseudomonal agents such as ceftazidime, piperacillin–tazobactam, ciprofloxacin, aminoglycosides, meropenem). Acinetobacter baumannii is oxidase-negative, a major multidrug-resistant hospital pathogen in ICUs.

Neisseria are oxidase-positive Gram-negative kidney-shaped diplococci, grown on chocolate agar or Thayer–Martin (modified New York City) medium in CO2. N. meningitidis ferments glucose and maltose; it causes epidemic meningitis in the African 'meningitis belt' (including northern Nigeria), especially in the dry season (serogroups A, C, W, X); CSF shows Gram-negative intracellular diplococci. N. gonorrhoeae ferments glucose only; it causes urethritis, cervicitis and ophthalmia neonatorum. Vibrio cholerae is a comma-shaped, oxidase-positive, highly motile ('darting') Gram-negative rod that grows on TCBS (yellow colonies) and in alkaline peptone water; its toxin causes 'rice-water' stools.
k: Meningococcus: glucose + maltose; gonococcus: glucose only
Vibrio: TCBS yellow colonies, darting motility

topics.title: Mycobacteria and Spore-forming Bacilli
topics.summary: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and leprae, Clostridium and Bacillus species.

notes.b: Mycobacteria have mycolic acid–rich cell walls and are acid-fast (Ziehl–Neelsen: red bacilli on a blue background; auramine fluorescence is more sensitive). M. tuberculosis grows slowly (generation time ~18 hours) on Lowenstein–Jensen medium (rough, buff 'cauliflower' colonies after 3–8 weeks) or faster in liquid MGIT culture; it is niacin-positive. GeneXpert MTB/RIF (a cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test) is the recommended initial test in Nigeria, detecting TB and rifampicin resistance within 2 hours. The Mantoux (tuberculin skin) test and IGRAs detect infection, not active disease. Nigeria has one of the highest TB burdens globally. M. leprae (leprosy) cannot be cultured in vitro; it grows in armadillos and mouse footpads; diagnosis uses slit-skin smears.
k: M. leprae cannot be cultured in vitro

notes.b: Clostridia are Gram-positive, spore-forming, anaerobic bacilli. C. tetani (terminal 'drumstick' spores) produces tetanospasmin, which blocks inhibitory neurotransmitter release (GABA and glycine), causing spastic paralysis, trismus and risus sardonicus; neonatal tetanus follows unhygienic cord care. C. perfringens causes gas gangrene (α-toxin, lecithinase — Nagler reaction) and food poisoning; C. botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release causing flaccid paralysis; C. difficile causes antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis. Bacillus anthracis (aerobic, non-motile, 'bamboo-stick' chains, 'medusa head' colonies) causes anthrax; B. cereus causes food poisoning from reheated rice.
k: C. tetani: drumstick spores, spastic paralysis
C. perfringens: gas gangrene, Nagler reaction

topics.title: Specimen Processing and Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing
topics.summary: Processing urine, blood, CSF and wound specimens; susceptibility testing and resistance detection.

notes.b: Urine: midstream specimen cultured quantitatively (calibrated loop); ≥ 10⁵ CFU/mL of a single organism indicates significant bacteriuria in a clean-catch sample (lower counts may be significant in catheter or symptomatic samples); media CLED (cystine–lactose–electrolyte-deficient — prevents Proteus swarming) or blood + MacConkey. Blood culture: aseptic collection of adequate volume (adults 8–10 mL per bottle, at least two sets from different sites) before antibiotics, incubated up to 5–7 days. CSF: urgent Gram stain, cell count, glucose and protein, culture on chocolate and blood agar; India ink or cryptococcal antigen for Cryptococcus in HIV. Pus and wound swabs: Gram stain and aerobic/anaerobic culture.
k: CSF: urgent Gram stain; India ink for Cryptococcus

notes.b: The Kirby–Bauer disc diffusion method uses Mueller–Hinton agar, a standardised inoculum (0.5 McFarland turbidity standard ≈ 1.5 × 10⁸ CFU/mL), antibiotic discs, incubation at 35–37 °C for 16–18 hours, and measurement of inhibition zones interpreted as susceptible, intermediate or resistant using CLSI or EUCAST breakpoints. MIC methods include broth microdilution and E-test gradient strips. Resistance detection: cefoxitin disc for MRSA; double-disc synergy test for ESBL (enhanced zone with clavulanate); modified carbapenem inactivation method (mCIM) for carbapenemases. Quality control uses reference strains (e.g. E. coli ATCC 25922, S. aureus ATCC 25923).
